content.text: Explain how seismic methods and a knowledge of wave properties have increased our understanding of the structure of Earth.
Build the answer around the two seismic wave types and the single property that separates them: one travels through liquids, the other does not.
Then use the way wave speed varies with density to deduce how the Earth's layers are arranged, and use the shadow zone to locate the core.
Every deduction about the Earth's structure must be tied to a specific wave observation, not merely asserted.

Seismic waves are generated by earthquakes and detected at the surface by seismographs. P (primary) waves are longitudinal and can pass through both solids and liquids, while S (secondary) waves are transverse and can travel only through solids. The absence of S waves from the shadow zone shows that the outer core is liquid. P waves travel faster in less dense material, so the way P and S wave speeds change with depth reveals that the crust is heterogeneous, that the mantle becomes denser with depth, and that there is a liquid outer core surrounding a solid inner core. Reflections and refractions of these waves at each boundary map out the layers, and measurements of their travel times have revealed the internal structure of the Earth, which cannot be probed directly.

Seismic methods work because an earthquake releases elastic energy that travels through the Earth as seismic waves, and because those waves change speed, direction and character at every boundary they meet. The two body wave types differ in exactly the way that makes the method possible.

P (primary) waves are longitudinal, produced by compression and rarefaction of the rock, so they can travel through solids, liquids and gases. S (secondary) waves are transverse, produced by shearing, and a shear stress cannot be supported in a fluid, so S waves travel only through solids. Earthquakes are detected at the surface by seismographs, which record the arrival time of each wave at each station, and those travel times are converted into depths.

The first deduction comes from the shadow zones. Stations between about $103^{\circ}$ and $143^{\circ}$ from the epicentre record P waves but no S waves. The refraction of P waves at the core-mantle boundary, taken together with this S-wave gap, shows that the outer core cannot be a solid: it is liquid, because S waves cannot pass through a fluid.

The second deduction uses the variation of wave speed with depth. Seismic waves travel faster in less dense, more rigid material, so the increase in P and S wave speed through the mantle shows that the mantle becomes denser and more rigid with depth, while the very low speeds in the crustal layers show that the crust is heterogeneous and in places partly molten near the top. Inside the outer core the P wave speed jumps sharply, indicating a liquid of much greater density, and the very small further increase in P wave speed near Earth's centre indicates a solid inner core, so the core is itself layered.

Every boundary is probed twice, by reflection and by refraction. A wave that reflects off a boundary returns after a known two-way travel time, which gives the depth directly, while a wave that refracts bends because its speed changes, and the amount of bending gives both the depth and the change in speed across the boundary. Measuring many such boundaries from all directions produces the layered model of a heterogeneous crust, a dense mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. That structure cannot be probed directly by any other means, and it could not have been known without a detailed understanding of how waves travel through materials.

content.text: X-rays.
Explain how X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube
An X-ray tube converts the kinetic energy of fast electrons into radiation, and there are two distinct ways this happens. A complete answer needs both mechanisms, not just the tube description.

For the comparison, ask what each picture is a view of: a shadow of the whole body, or a thin slice through it? Overlapping structures are superimposed in one and separated in the other, which is exactly why one of them shows soft tissue and the other does not.

Electrons are emitted by a heated filament and accelerated through a large potential difference onto a metal (tungsten) target. Braking or bremsstrahlung radiation is produced as the electrons are decelerated in the electric field of the target nuclei, giving X-rays over a continuous range of wavelengths; characteristic radiation is produced when an incoming electron ejects an inner-shell electron and an outer-shell electron drops into the gap, emitting X-rays of wavelength characteristic of the target element.

Current in the filament heats it to incandescence and emits electrons by thermionic emission. A large potential difference between cathode and anode accelerates them to high speed, so most of their energy is lost abruptly in the target. Two processes convert that kinetic energy into X-rays. In bremsstrahlung, an electron is decelerated in the electric field of a target nucleus, radiating at each stage of the deceleration; because the deceleration can take any value, this gives a continuous spectrum up to a short-wavelength cutoff set by the accelerating voltage. In characteristic emission, an incoming electron has enough energy to knock an electron out of an inner shell of the target atom; an electron from a higher shell then drops down to fill the vacancy and emits an X-ray photon whose energy equals the difference between the two shell energies, which is characteristic of the target element.

content.text: Explain why MRI is an effective tool for diagnosing brain tumours.
Start from what the MRI image is actually a map of. It is not a density of tissue in the x-ray sense; it is a density of hydrogen nuclei, and hydrogen nuclei are found almost entirely in water.
So the question becomes a comparison: how does the water content of a tumour differ from that of the healthy brain tissue around it, and how does that difference show up in the image?

A brain tumour is a region of abnormal tissue with a different (greater) water and therefore hydrogen nucleus content from the surrounding healthy tissue. MRI produces an image by measuring the density of hydrogen (protons) in the body, so the region of altered hydrogen density corresponding to the tumour stands out against the normal tissue, allowing the tumour to be located and its extent determined.

An MRI scanner first places the body in a strong, static magnetic field, which aligns the magnetic moments of the hydrogen nuclei (protons) in the water of the tissues. A pulse of radio waves at the Larmor frequency tips the aligned moments out of alignment, and as the protons precess and relax back they emit radio waves whose frequency is set by their position in the field. A computer combines the signals into an image, so the brightness of each point in the image is a measure of the density of hydrogen nuclei there.

A brain tumour is a region of abnormal tissue with rapid, uncontrolled cell division and elevated metabolic rate, and it holds more water - and therefore more hydrogen nuclei - than the surrounding healthy brain tissue. Because the image is a map of hydrogen nucleus density, that region produces a signal that differs from the normal tissue around it and shows up as a distinctly differentiated, brighter area in the scan. MRI can therefore distinguish a tumour from the surrounding tissue, locate it and measure how far it extends, which is why it is an effective diagnostic tool for brain tumours.

content.text: With reference to coherent and incoherent bundles of fibres, explain how an endoscope is used to observe internal organs.

Both bundles are doing the same physics: each fibre guides light by repeated total internal reflection at the glass-air boundary between its core and its cladding. The only difference between them is how the fibres are arranged.
Ask of each bundle what its arrangement has to guarantee. Does the light need to arrive at the right end only, or does it also have to arrive at the right place?

An endoscope contains two bundles of optical fibres. The incoherent (illuminating) bundle has its fibres arranged randomly; it carries light from the lamp at the outer end of the endoscope to the tip, illuminating the internal organ. The coherent (image) bundle has its fibres arranged in the same orderly positions and orientations at both ends; light reflected from the organ enters the fibre that illuminated that point of the organ and emerges from the same position at the eyepiece, so an image of the organ is transmitted to the observer's eye or camera.

Light entering an optical fibre at an angle greater than the critical angle is totally internally reflected at the boundary between the glass core and the surrounding cladding, and is guided along the fibre even round sharp bends. A fibre optic endoscope is a flexible sealed tube containing two bundles of such fibres.

The incoherent (illuminating) bundle has its fibres arranged randomly, so light from a lamp at the outer end is scrambled on the way in. This does not matter, because no image has to be preserved: the bundle simply delivers a large area of bright light to the distal tip, where a lens spreads it over the internal organ being examined.

The coherent (image) bundle has each fibre in the same position and orientation at both ends, so a point on the organ that is lit sends its reflected light into one particular fibre at the distal end and that same fibre delivers it to the same position at the proximal end. The pattern of illuminated fibres at the eyepiece therefore reconstructs an image of the organ, which the observer views or a camera records. So the incoherent bundle illuminates the organ and the coherent bundle transmits the image of the organ to the eye, and together they let an internal organ be observed directly.

content.text: An increased understanding of the properties of radioactive isotopes has been important in the development of medical technologies used to analyse bodily processes.
Justify this statement.

You need at least two scanning techniques that use a radioisotope, and for each one you must name the specific property of the isotope that makes it work - the type of radiation, the energy, or the half-life.

For each technique also state what the tracer is taken up by or attached to, and how the detected radiation becomes an image. That uptake mechanism is what turns the position of the isotope into a record of a bodily process rather than just a picture of an organ.

Radioisotopes emit radiation that can be detected outside the body, and their half-lives can be chosen to be long enough to last through a scan but short enough that the patient is not exposed for long. A radioisotope introduced into the body is carried by the blood or absorbed by particular organs, so its position traces a bodily process: in a thyroid scan ${}^{131}\mathrm{I}$ is taken up by the thyroid, and in PET a positron-emitting isotope such as ${}^{18}\mathrm{F}$ is attached to a molecule taken up by the tissue of interest. The emitted radiation is detected and an image of the organ, or of the flow of the tracer, is built up, so the function of the organ and the presence of disease can be assessed. Our understanding of emission, penetration and half-life also allows safe tracer doses and correctly timed scans.

Two properties of radioisotopes make medical imaging possible. First, the radiation they emit can leave the body and be detected outside it: gamma rays penetrate tissue and ionise very few molecules, and in PET the positron emitted by the isotope annihilates with an electron in the body to produce a pair of gamma rays travelling in opposite directions. Second, the half-life can be chosen: long enough for the isotope to be produced, transported, taken up and imaged, but short enough that it decays away soon afterwards so the dose to the patient is small. Six to eight hours, as for technetium-99m, is typical.

A bone scan exploits selective uptake: technetium-99m, a gamma emitter with a six hour half-life, is injected as a labelled compound and is taken up preferentially by bone that is actively remodelling. Regions of abnormal turnover, such as a bone tumour or a stress fracture, take up far more of the tracer and appear as hotspots against the background, so the scan maps bone metabolism rather than bone shape.

A PET scan exploits positron emission and chemical specificity: fluorine-18 (110 minute half-life) is incorporated into FDG, a glucose analogue, and the tracer follows glucose metabolism. The brain uses a great deal of glucose, so FDG concentrates there and the coincidence-detected annihilation gamma rays map brain function and expose abnormal metabolism. The image is therefore a quantitative record of how the organ is functioning. Because the same understanding of emission, penetration and half-life is what allows a tracer dose to be chosen that is diagnostic yet safe, the properties of radioactive isotopes are exactly what made these medical technologies possible, which justifies the statement.

content.text: Parsecs, and the resolution and sensitivity of telescopes.

For the definition, remember that a parsec is built from the geometry of Earth's orbit: a right triangle with a baseline of 1 AU and a very small angle at the star. Draw it and label the sides and the angle.

For Galileo, do not just define resolution and sensitivity. The question asks which one was limiting for the objects he actually looked at, so bring the small size of his objective lens and the brightness of those objects into the argument.
For the technology, the question wants a description of how it works and why that improves resolution, not just a name.

items: (a)(i) The parsec is the distance to a star at which the Earth's orbital radius, 1 AU, subtends an angle of one second of arc, equivalently the distance at which a star shows a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond. Diagram: a long thin right-angled triangle with the Sun at one vertex, the star at the opposite vertex and the 1 AU baseline at the third, with the angle of 1 arcsecond marked at the star. $1\,\mathrm{pc} = 3.26$ light years.

(a)(ii) Resolution is the ability to distinguish two separate objects or features close together, and it improves only with a larger objective lens or greater aperture. Galileo's objective was small, so his resolution was poor: planets appeared as small discs of light rather than resolved bodies, and Saturn's rings looked like handles because the ring and the moons could not be separated. Sensitivity is the ability to detect a faint object, and although his instrument collected little light he was viewing the Moon, Jupiter's moons and bright stars, which are not faint, so extra light-gathering would not have added detail. Resolution was therefore the limiting factor in his observations.

(a)(iii) Adaptive optics: a small bright guide star in the field of view is used to measure the wavefront distortions caused by the Earth's atmosphere, and a rapidly deformable mirror is continuously adjusted to cancel them, so the image forms as if the atmosphere were absent. Removing the atmospheric blurring allows much finer angular detail, and hence close double stars and small moons, to be resolved.

content.text: Part (a)(i) is a definition that must be tied to the diagram. The apparent position of a nearby star shifts against the distant background as Earth moves around the Sun, and the total shift over six months is twice the parallax angle, 2p. The geometry is a very long thin right triangle in which the side of length 1 AU, the radius of Earth's orbit, subtends the angle p at the star, so p is approximately 1 divided by the distance in AU. By definition the parsec is the distance at which p equals 1 arcsecond, and since 1 radian is 206265 arcseconds, 1 pc = 206265 AU = 3.26 light years. Both the diagram and the definition must be present for the top mark.

Part (a)(ii) needs the two definitions, a reason for each, and a link to the actual observations. Resolution is limited by diffraction at the objective, so it depends only on aperture; Galileo's objective was a few centimetres across, which is why his planets stayed as unresolved discs and why Saturn's ring could not be separated from the planet's moons. Sensitivity depends on the light gathered, so it too depends on aperture, but it also depends on the brightness of the target, and the objects Galileo chose, the Moon, Jupiter's moons and bright stars, are all bright. A larger aperture would therefore have made his images brighter, which was not what was limiting his results, whereas it would have improved his resolution, which was. That is the sense in which resolution was the more important property for his observations.

Part (a)(iii) must explain the mechanism, because a name alone earns only the lower mark. The star's light reaching the ground has passed through a turbulent atmosphere, so the wavefront is distorted by cells of varying refractive index, which scatter light from each point of the object over a small patch and blur the image. A wavefront sensor measures this distortion many times a second, either from a bright natural guide star or by shining a laser into the guide star itself, and a deformable mirror with many independently driven segments is adjusted continuously to impose the opposite distortion, so the emerging wavefront is planar and the image forms as if the atmosphere were absent. Since the remaining limit is then diffraction at the telescope aperture, much finer angular detail, and hence close double stars and small moons, can be resolved.

content.text: Using a Cepheid and one other named example, explain the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic variable stars.

The distinction is where the cause of the variation lies: inside the star, or outside it. Test each example against that question. Does the total energy emitted by the system change, or only the amount that reaches us?

For the examples themselves, a Cepheid pulses, while an eclipsing binary has one star pass in front of the other along our line of sight. Name both, and say in each case which quantity actually changes.

An intrinsic variable star varies in brightness because of changes within the star itself: a Cepheid variable pulses, contracting and expanding, with its outer layers heating and cooling so its luminosity really does change. An extrinsic variable star varies only in apparent brightness because something external changes: an eclipsing binary (a double star in which one star passes in front of the other from our line of sight) changes the total light reaching us although the luminosity of each star is unchanged. The period of a Cepheid is linked to its mean luminosity, which is what makes it so useful for measuring distances.

The test for the two categories is where the cause of the observed variation lies. An intrinsic variable produces a genuinely changing total radiated power, because the star itself is doing something different. An extrinsic variable has an unchanged total output, and only the amount of light that reaches the observer changes, because something external blocks, passes, or changes the colour of the light.

A Cepheid is intrinsic. It passes through a pulsation cycle, contracting and expanding; as it contracts the outer layers are heated, more of the fusion energy is radiated away from the surface, the radius changes, and both the luminosity and the colour therefore change over the cycle. The energy source is nuclear fusion throughout, but the rate at which that energy escapes varies, and the period of pulsation is linked to the mean luminosity in a way that makes Cepheids useful as distance indicators.

An eclipsing binary is extrinsic. Two stars orbit a common centre of mass, and when their line of sight takes one in front of the other the projected area of the fainter star is blocked, so the total flux received falls and recovers as the star moves clear. Neither star's internal structure, radius, temperature or total luminosity changes at all; only the apparent brightness changes, and only by a small fraction. Because the light is only partly blocked, eclipsing binaries have shallower, box-shaped light curves than pulsating variables, which is how the two are distinguished observationally.

content.text: Spectroscopy is an important tool in obtaining information about stars, but it is a much more powerful tool when combined with photometry.
Justify this statement.
A justification needs a limitation, not just two descriptions. The test question is: what can spectroscopy NOT tell you about a star, and what does photometry not tell you?
Then give at least one worked example where putting the two together yields something neither gives alone, for instance motion plus distance, or a light curve plus a spectral type.

Spectroscopy splits the light from a star into its component wavelengths. Unique absorption lines identify the chemical elements present in the star's atmosphere, the strengths and widths of the lines reveal temperature, pressure and rotation, and a Doppler shift of the lines gives the star's velocity towards or away from us. However, spectroscopy alone gives no information about how bright the star is, and even the best spectra give no direct distance. Photometry measures the total radiant flux received at the detector, so it provides the apparent magnitude and hence, with an assumed absolute magnitude, the distance, and it provides accurate brightness values for light curves. Combined, the two give a far more complete picture: the spectrum identifies the elements and the Doppler shift gives the motion, while the photometry, converted to absolute magnitude, places the star on the H-R diagram so that its temperature (from colour index B-V), luminosity, radius and evolutionary stage can be deduced. For example, a spectroscopic radial velocity plus a photometric distance gives a star's space velocity, and variable-star photometry combined with a spectral type identifies a Cepheid and calibrates the period-luminosity relation used to measure distances to other galaxies.

The statement can only be justified once the two techniques are compared, because each measures a different physical quantity. Spectroscopy measures the distribution of photon energy arriving at the detector, that is which wavelengths are present. Photometry measures the total radiant flux arriving, that is how much energy per second per unit area is reaching the telescope.

Spectroscopy is powerful but limited. Because atomic energy levels are quantised, the pattern of absorption lines is a unique fingerprint, so the chemical composition follows, and the line widths and strengths give pressure, density, rotation and surface gravity, while a displacement of the whole pattern is a Doppler shift that gives the radial velocity. What spectroscopy cannot give is any measure of how bright the star is: a very luminous star 100 light years away and a dim one 1 light year away can present identical spectra. Nor does it give a distance, because the intensity has been reduced by exactly the unknown factor it is being used to find.

Photometry is powerful but also limited. It gives the apparent magnitude, and with an assumed absolute magnitude from a spectral type it gives a distance, and it also produces the accurate light curves needed to classify variables. It cannot identify the elements and it cannot give a velocity. Combining them closes both gaps, and the combination adds information that neither has alone. The colour index from photometric photometry is a proxy for temperature, so combined with the absolute magnitude it places the star on the H-R diagram, which then fixes radius, luminosity and evolutionary stage; the Doppler shift from the spectrum combined with the distance from the photometry gives the star's space velocity and hence its membership of the Galaxy; and a light curve combined with a spectral type identifies a Cepheid and calibrates the period-luminosity relation that is then used to measure distances to other galaxies. That is why the combination is much more powerful than spectroscopy alone.

content.text: Name a radioisotope used in agriculture and describe its use.
Agricultural radioisotopes are used in two quite different ways: as tracers that follow where something goes, and as sources that irradiate the plant or the produce. Either will do for full marks.

For a tracer, the essential feature is that the isotope behaves chemically like the ordinary element, so it can take part in the same processes, while still being detectable because it is radioactive.
Say how the radiation is detected, and what that detection then reveals about the plant.

Example: radioactive phosphorus-32 is used as a tracer in fertiliser. It is applied in a fertiliser to a crop and a Geiger counter is used to detect the radiation from the labelled atoms, showing where the absorbed phosphate has gone in the plant and how the plant takes up fertiliser. Gamma-emitting cobalt-60 is also used to irradiate seed to induce mutations that improve crop yields, and to sterilise or extend the shelf life of produce.

Two marks are available here: one for naming an isotope that is used in agriculture and one for describing its use, so the answer has to do both. A complete description of a tracer use gives the isotope, the element whose behaviour it imitates, where it is applied, and how the radiation is detected and what that reveals. Radioactive phosphorus-32 is the standard example: it is chemically identical to ordinary phosphate, so it can be added to fertiliser and absorbed by the crop in the normal way, and because it is radioactive the phosphate that has been taken up can be tracked with a Geiger-Muller counter placed over the plant, showing both how much fertiliser the plant absorbs and where that phosphate ends up inside it.

A contrasting use, which also earns both marks, is gamma-emitting cobalt-60 to irradiate seed: the radiation induces mutations in the genetic material of the seed, and those mutations are then selected for desirable characteristics such as disease resistance, which raises crop yields. The same isotope is used to irradiate fruit and vegetables to kill or sterilise the microorganisms that cause spoilage, extending shelf life without the use of chemical preservatives. Either example answers the question, provided both the isotope and the use are named.

content.text: Explain how the reaction rate in a nuclear reactor can be increased or decreased.

Three separate quantities control the rate, and the marks need all three related to the rate of fission: the energies of the neutrons, the moderator that sets those energies, and the control rods that remove neutrons.
Ask first what has to be true of a neutron before a uranium-235 nucleus will capture it, then what the moderator is for, then which direction the control rods must move to slow the reaction down.
For (ii), check the equation first by adding the mass numbers and then the atomic numbers on each side, and then compare the *actual* masses, not the mass numbers, of reactants and products.

** Fission is caused by a neutron being captured by a uranium-235 nucleus, and the probability of capture is far higher for a slow (thermal) neutron than for a fast one, so the reactor contains a **moderator** - heavy water, graphite or ordinary water - with which the fast neutrons produced by fission collide repeatedly and lose energy. The better the moderator, the more thermal neutrons are produced inside the fuel and the faster the chain reaction runs. The rate is then set by the **control rods**: rods made of cadmium, boron or hafnium absorb neutrons strongly, so pushing them further into the reactor vessel removes more neutrons and slows or stops the reaction, while withdrawing them lets more neutrons remain free to be captured and speeds the reaction up. With the rods fully inserted the chain reaction is shut down. Raising the enrichment of the fuel, or using a better moderator, increases the rate in the same way.
**
Part

. Three factors must each be related to the rate of reaction. First, the neutrons themselves: they must be slow for capture by $\,{}^{235}\mathrm{U}$ to be likely, whereas the neutrons born in each fission are fast. Second, the moderator: a good moderator removes energy from fast neutrons efficiently, so a greater fraction of the neutrons in the fuel reach thermal speeds inside the fuel where they can be captured, and the rate of fission rises. Third, the control rods: these are made of a strong neutron absorber, so the number of neutrons available for capture is set by how much absorber is in the reactor vessel. Inserting the rods further removes more neutrons and reduces the rate, withdrawing them increases it, and with them fully inserted the chain reaction is stopped. In every case the relationship is the same - the rate of fission, and therefore the rate at which energy is produced, is proportional to the number of free neutrons available to be captured.

content.text: Explain why energy is released in this reaction.

** The total mass of the products, $\,{}^{140}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}\mathrm{Kr} + 4n$, is **slightly less** than the total mass of the reactants, $\,{}^{235}\mathrm{U} + n$. The mass that is missing has not been destroyed; it has been converted into the kinetic energy of the two daughter nuclei and of the four neutrons and into the radiation, mostly gamma rays, that accompanies the fission. By Einstein's relation $E = mc^{2}$ that small mass defect corresponds to a very large quantity of energy, because $c^{2}$ is an enormous number, which is why a mass change of a fraction of a percent of an atomic mass unit still releases about 200 MeV per event.

. Check the equation before using it. Mass numbers: $235 + 1 = 236$ on the left and $140 + 92 + 4 = 236$ on the right. Charge numbers: $92 + 0 = 92$ on the left and $56 + 36 = 92$ on the right. The equation is therefore balanced, but balance of mass numbers is not the same as balance of mass. The measured masses of the products are slightly smaller than the measured masses of the reactants, and the difference is the mass defect. It appears as kinetic energy of the fragments and of the neutrons and as gamma radiation. Applying $E = mc^{2}$ with $c^{2} = 9.0\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-2}}$ shows why a mass defect of a fraction of a percent of an atomic mass unit, about $1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, still yields an energy of order $2\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, roughly 200 MeV.

content.text: Copy and complete in your booklet the following table comparing forces in the atomic nucleus.
Do the table one force at a time. For the electrostatic force ask two separate questions: does it push or pull, and how far does it reach?

Compare that range with the strong nuclear force's. The strong force acts only across a distance comparable with a nucleus, which is exactly why it cannot hold a proton at one end of a large nucleus to a proton at the other end.
The gravitational column is supplied as a reference. Use it to order the three forces by strength, and remember that only one of the three has a range limited to nuclear dimensions.

items: Electrostatic: high strength, repulsive, long range - the repulsion between protons acts right across the nucleus and beyond, not only between neighbouring nucleons.
Strong: very high strength, attractive, short range - of the order of $1\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, the size of a nucleus.
Gravitational (given in the paper): low strength, attractive, infinite range.

content.text: The gravitational column is supplied in the paper (low strength, attractive, infinite range) and is the reference for relative strength and range. For the electrostatic force the repulsion between protons is enormously stronger than gravity, it is repulsive, and it acts at long range: like gravity it operates throughout the nucleus and beyond, so every proton repels every other proton and not merely its nearest neighbours. For the strong nuclear force the attraction is by far the strongest of the three, it is attractive between all pairs of nucleons, protons and neutrons alike, and its range is only of the order of a femtometre, the size of a nucleus.

items: Electrostatic: high strength, repulsive, long range (it acts throughout the nucleus and beyond).
Strong: very high strength, attractive, short range (about $1\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, the size of a nucleus).

content.text: The contrast between the two ranges is the physics that matters. Because the strong force is short range it holds each nucleon only to its immediate neighbours, whereas the electrostatic repulsion accumulates over the whole nucleus; a stable nucleus therefore needs neutrons, which add strong-force attraction without adding any electrostatic repulsion, and a nucleus with too high a proportion of protons becomes unstable and decays away.

content.text: A cricket ball has a mass of 156 g and a velocity of $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength.
The de Broglie wavelength of a macroscopic object comes from the same relation as for an electron, $\lambda = h/mv$, but the mass term behaves in a completely different way.

Convert the mass to kilograms before substituting. A factor of a thousand in the mass changes the answer by a factor of a thousand, and this question is really about what that does to the size of the wavelength.
When you have the wavelength, compare it with the size of the ball itself. That comparison, not the arithmetic, is the point of the question.

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{(0.156)(20)} = 2.12 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{m}$, about $2.1 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{m}$, which is so small that the wave nature of the ball is unobservable.
Substitute the data sheet value of $h$, convert the mass from grams to kilograms, and use the given velocity.

The result is about $2.1\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{m}$, some $10^{26}$ times smaller than the diameter of the ball and many orders of magnitude smaller than a nucleus. This is why the wave nature of a cricket ball cannot be observed: the diffraction and interference that would reveal it require slits or obstacles comparable in size with the wavelength, and nothing on that scale exists here. The same formula applied to an electron of mass $9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ moving at $10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives a wavelength of about $7\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$, comparable with the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is the scale on which electron diffraction experiments are actually performed.

1 mark: correct final answer, $2.12 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{m}$, with correct units

content.text: Identify the types and number of quarks and leptons in a tritium (${}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}$) atom.
A tritium atom has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus, and one electron outside it. Start by building each nucleon out of quarks.
Recall the quark composition of a proton and of a neutron, and then add them up for the whole nucleus rather than for a single nucleon.
Count the leptons separately at the end: the electron is the only lepton, and neither a proton nor a neutron contains one.

A tritium atom has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus and one electron. A proton is two up quarks and one down quark; each neutron is one up quark and two down quarks. So the nucleus contains 4 up quarks and 5 down quarks in total, and the atom has 1 lepton, the electron. (Total 9 valence quarks, 3 from each of the 3 nucleons, plus 1 lepton.)
A tritium nucleus, $\,{}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}$, contains one proton and two neutrons. A proton is two up quarks and one down quark; a neutron is one up quark and two down quarks.

Adding the three nucleons gives $1\times(2u+1d) + 2\times(1u+2d) = 4u + 5d$, so the nucleus contains 4 up quarks and 5 down quarks, 9 valence quarks in total. The single electron outside the nucleus is the one lepton, and since neither a proton nor a neutron contains a lepton there are no others.

A useful check on the count is the charge. Each up quark carries $+\tfrac{2}{3}e$ and each down quark carries $-\tfrac{1}{3}e$, so $4\left(+\tfrac{2}{3}\right) + 5\left(-\tfrac{1}{3}\right) = \tfrac{8}{3} - \tfrac{5}{3} = +1$, which is the charge of the tritium nucleus, as it must be.

content.text: Outline the main contributions of Heisenberg and Pauli to the development of atomic theory.
Two physicists and two contributions each. Decide for each scientist what the single most important thing was that he produced.

For Heisenberg, ask what the uncertainty principle says about knowing the position and the momentum of a particle at the same time, and what that does to the classical picture of an electron in a definite orbit.
For Pauli, ask what would happen if two electrons in an atom were allowed to have the same set of quantum numbers, and connect your answer to the shape of the periodic table.

Werner Heisenberg developed matrix mechanics, the first complete formulation of quantum mechanics, and formulated the uncertainty principle, which states that the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly at the same time. This set a fundamental limit on the classical picture of an electron in a definite orbit and supported the replacement of orbits by energy levels. Wolfgang Pauli formulated the exclusion principle, which states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. This explains how the electrons fill the available energy levels, why the outermost level of a heavy atom holds only one or two electrons (giving the alkali metals and the noble gases) and hence the structure of the periodic table, and why matter is stable against collapse.

Heisenberg's two contributions are matrix mechanics, the first complete formulation of quantum mechanics, and the uncertainty principle, $\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2$, which states that the position and the momentum of a particle cannot both be defined precisely at the same time. The uncertainty principle removes the last part of the classical picture, in which a particle has a definite orbit with a definite position and a definite speed, and it is one of the reasons the electron in an atom had to be replaced by an electron on an energy level described by a probability distribution. It is also part of the reason an atom does not collapse.

Pauli's contribution is the exclusion principle, which states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. Electrons must therefore fill the available states one at a time, lowest energy first, which explains how the shells of an atom are built up, why the outermost shell of a heavy atom can hold only one or two electrons - giving the highly reactive alkali metals and the halogens - and why the noble gases, with full outer shells, are unreactive. That is the origin of the structure of the periodic table, and the exclusion principle is also part of the reason matter is stable.

2 marks: accurately outlines two contributions.

content.text: Mathematical models, validated by experimental evidence, have improved our understanding of the atom.
Justify this statement, focusing on the models developed by Bohr and de Broglie.

A model is validated when a measurement agrees with something the model predicted, so for each of your two models write the prediction down first and the experimental test down second, and do not reverse the order.

For Bohr, the predictions to quote are the pattern of the hydrogen spectrum and the value of the ionisation energy; for de Broglie, the prediction is that the electron should behave as a wave, with a wavelength set by its momentum.
Finish by saying what the two models together replaced, and how the modern picture differs from Bohr's idea of a definite orbit.

Bohr's model treated the electron as moving in fixed circular orbits for which angular momentum is quantised, $mvr = nh/2\pi$, so the energy of each orbit is quantised, $E_n = -E_1/n^{2}$. This mathematical model was validated by the agreement of the predicted hydrogen line spectrum and hydrogen ionisation energy with experiment, and by the success of the Rydberg formula $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^{2} - 1/n_i^{2})$, which correctly predicted that the hydrogen spectrum consists of discrete lines rather than a continuous spread. de Broglie's model proposed that matter has a wave nature, $\lambda = h/mv$, and applied the idea of standing waves to the electron in the atom, so that only orbits corresponding to a whole number of wavelengths around the circumference are allowed and the electron energies are quantised. The model was validated by the observed electron diffraction patterns, in which electrons are diffracted by a crystal lattice exactly as waves are, and by the fact that the quantised energies it predicts agree with observed atomic spectra. Together these mathematical models, confirmed by experiment, replaced the classical nuclear model and produced the modern quantum (wave) model of the atom, in which the electron is described by a standing wave and its energy by a probability distribution.

The statement makes three claims that each have to be supported: that the models are mathematical, that they were validated by experimental evidence, and that they improved our understanding of the atom. Bohr's model is mathematical in that it quantises the angular momentum, $mvr = nh/2\pi$, and derives the hydrogen spectrum from that quantisation. It was validated by measurement: the wavelengths predicted for the Balmer series from $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ agree with the observed line spectrum, including the fact that the spectrum consists of discrete lines and not a continuous spread, and the predicted ionisation energy of hydrogen agrees with the measured value.

de Broglie's model is mathematical in that it applies $p = h/\lambda$ to the electron and then requires $2\pi r = n\lambda$, which reduces to Bohr's quantisation but now explains it: only those orbits are physically possible, and each is a stationary state. It was validated by the observation of electron diffraction, in which a beam of electrons is diffracted by a crystal lattice in exactly the way that light is diffracted by a grating, and by the agreement of the quantised energies the model implies with the observed atomic spectra.

Together these models replaced the classical nuclear model, in which the electron was supposed to orbit like a planet and should therefore have radiated and collapsed the atom, with the quantum model in which the electron is described by a standing wave in a probability distribution and its energy by one of a set of discrete levels. The justification is therefore that both models were quantitative, both made testable predictions, and those predictions were confirmed by experiment - which is exactly what the statement claims.

content.text: Construct a truth table for the logic circuit contained in Section D.

Section D contains only two elements: a NOT gate on one of the comparator outputs and an AND gate. Write the output as a single Boolean expression in $I_0$ and $I_1$ before you fill in any table entries.

$O_0 = \overline{I_0} \cdot I_1$, so the output is 1 only when $I_0 = 0$ and $I_1 = 1$.
The upper comparator output $I_0$ is fed through an inverter, so the first input to the AND gate is $\overline{I_0}$. The lower comparator output $I_1$ enters the AND gate directly.
Evaluating for the four input combinations gives the table above. The output is 1 only when the inverter's input is 0, so that $\overline{I_0} = 1$, and the AND gate's other input is also 1.

A common wrong reading is to ignore the inverter and treat the gate as a plain AND of the two comparator outputs, which would make $O_0 = 1$ when both are 1. content.text: Explain whether the operational amplifiers in Section C of the circuit are used in an open loop or closed loop configuration.
Trace the wires from each amplifier's output and ask whether any of them returns to one of that amplifier's own inputs. That single question settles the configuration.

Once you know there is no return path, think about what an amplifier does with an enormous voltage gain: even a millivolt between the inputs is enough to drive the output hard against one of the supply rails, so the device acts as a switch rather than as an analogue amplifier.

The operational amplifiers are used in an open loop configuration. In a closed loop configuration some of the output is fed back to the input, but here there is no feedback path: the output of each amplifier goes only to the logic circuit in Section D, so the amplifiers operate open loop and act as comparators.

A closed loop (negative feedback) configuration is one in which part of the output signal is fed back to an input, so the gain is set by the network of resistors around the amplifier rather than by the amplifier itself.

In Section C neither amplifier has any such path. Each output node $I_0$ and $I_1$ runs forward only, into the inverter and the AND gate in Section D. There is nothing returning to either input terminal, so the amplifiers are used in an open loop configuration.

The consequence of open loop operation is what makes this circuit work. With gain approaching infinity the output of each amplifier saturates at one of its supply rails, $+5\ \mathrm{V}$ or $0\ \mathrm{V}$, so each amplifier converts the small voltage difference between its inputs into a clean logic level. That is why the outputs can be fed straight into the gates of Section D without any level conversion, and it is why the amplifier is acting as a comparator here.

content.text: Light-emitting diodes and optical fibres.
This part has two halves about two different devices. Answer each half separately rather than writing one continuous paragraph, because the marks are split between them.

For the LED, the ideas you need are the p-type and n-type layers, what forward bias does to the junction, and what happens when an electron meets a hole there. For the optical fibre, the ideas are the core and the cladding and the condition on the angle at which light strikes their boundary.
The detailed material properties of silica that make the fibre work are the subject of part (f), so keep that material for part (f) and concentrate here on how each device works.

items: (i) A light-emitting diode is a p-n junction formed in a semiconductor such as gallium arsenide or gallium phosphide. When it is forward biased the depletion layer narrows, electrons from the n-type region and holes from the p-type region are forced together, and where they recombine at the junction the energy released appears as photons, $E = hf$, with $f$ fixed by the band gap of the compound used. Almost all of the electrical energy goes into light rather than heat, and no filament burns out, so the device is small, efficient and long lived.

(ii) An optical fibre carries information as light. An LED or laser at one end converts the electrical signal into pulses of light, and the light stays in the core by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary until it emerges at the far end, where a photodiode turns it back into an electrical signal.

content.text: Sub-part (i), the LED. Doping silicon or a III-V compound semiconductor produces two regions, an n-type region rich in free electrons and a p-type region rich in holes. Where they meet there is a depletion region containing almost no charge carriers, and this is the p-n junction.

Applying a forward bias, positive to the p-type side, narrows that depletion region and pushes carriers across it. Electrons injected into the p-type region meet holes there and recombine. In an ordinary diode this recombination energy is released as heat; in a light-emitting diode the material is chosen so that a direct band gap lets the energy be released as a photon instead.

The photon frequency, and therefore the colour, is fixed by the band gap of the compound, which is why different materials give red, amber, green or blue diodes. Because almost all of the input energy leaves as light rather than as heat, an LED runs cool, needs only a few milliamps, switches on and off quickly, and has no filament to fail.

Sub-part (ii), the optical fibre. The fibre is a core of glass with a slightly higher refractive index surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering the core at an angle greater than the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary is totally internally reflected and so cannot escape.

Because the reflection is total, essentially no light leaves sideways however much the fibre is bent, so the light travels many kilometres with very little loss and the signal cannot be picked up from outside the fibre. An LED or laser launches the signal as light pulses at one end and a photodiode converts it back to an electrical signal at the other.

content.text: What properties of silica make it a suitable material for use in optical fibres?

Sort the required properties into optical ones and mechanical or chemical ones. The optical properties decide whether the light stays in the fibre and whether it survives the journey; the others decide whether the fibre can be drawn into long, thin, strong strands that survive being laid.

For the guiding property you need two refractive indices, the core and the cladding, and a condition on the angle of incidence at the boundary between them. For the transparency property think about which part of the spectrum has to be used for telecommunications and how far ordinary glass would attenuate it.
Three distinct, clearly stated properties earn the full marks. General statements such as 'it is a good material' do not, so name the property and say what it does for the fibre.

Silica glass is transparent: it has very low absorption and scattering of visible light and of the near infrared, so light can travel many kilometres along a fibre with little attenuation. It has a sufficiently high refractive index that light striking the core-glass/cladding boundary above the critical angle is totally internally reflected, so the light is guided along the core rather than escaping. It can be drawn into very fine, flexible, strong fibres, and it is chemically inert and unaffected by moisture, heat or most chemicals, so the fibre is durable.

Property 1, transparency. The glass must have negligible absorption and scattering at the wavelengths actually used. Telecommunications fibres are made of very pure fused silica, which transmits the near infra-red (around 850, 1300 and 1550 nm) with losses of only a fraction of a decibel per kilometre, so a signal can cross an ocean without amplification.

Property 2, the refractive index difference between core and cladding. The core must have a slightly higher refractive index than the cladding, so that light meeting the boundary at more than the critical angle is totally internally reflected and is guided along the core rather than refracting out of it.

Total internal reflection also survives bending, so a flexible cable can follow a building or an ocean floor while keeping the light inside the core, and because the reflection is total very little of the signal escapes sideways.

Property 3, mechanical strength and drawability. Molten silica can be drawn into fibres only a few micrometres in diameter that are nevertheless stronger than steel of the same diameter, and with no plasticisers or solvents in the glass the mechanical properties do not change with age or with exposure to moisture, so the fibre stays flexible and strong.

Property 4, chemical durability. Fused silica is chemically inert and is attacked by almost no chemicals, so the fibre is not damaged by water, by most solvents or by most acids, which is what allows cables to be installed underground, underwater or in a human body without a protective jacket doing all the work.

items: 3 marks: identifies in clear language three key optical properties that are desirable.
2 marks: identifies at least two key optical properties that are desirable.
1 mark: shows understanding of the desirable optical properties.

content.text: The semiconductor integrated circuit industry is rapidly approaching fundamental physics limitations for the design of integrated circuits for computers.
Explain what these limitations are and why this will require a reconceptualisation of the way computers are designed.

Organise the answer as separate physical limits rather than one long list. Good headings are the size of the transistor, the heat produced, the speed at which signals can move along the wires, and the quantum limit.

For each limit write the sentence 'this stops being improvable when ...' and then say what it prevents the chip from doing. The mark is for the physics together with its consequence, not for naming a phenomenon.

The question ends with a judgement, so your list of limits has to lead somewhere: it must explain why simply making today's architecture smaller and faster can no longer be the answer, and what will have to change instead.

Size limitation: a transistor cannot be made much smaller than a few atoms, and as the gate length approaches the atomic scale electrons tunnel through the insulating gate layer, so the current leaks even when the transistor is nominally off, and further shrinking stops working and also leaves no room for the wires. Heat: every switching event dissipates energy, so as more switches operate faster on a smaller chip the power density rises and the chip overheats, so the clock speed cannot be raised indefinitely. Speed of the carriers: electrons travel only so fast through silicon, and the time taken to charge and discharge each node sets the shortest possible clock period. Quantum: the uncertainty principle puts a limit on how well the position and momentum of an electron can be known, so a charge cannot be confined to a region much smaller than a wavelength. These limits mean that simply making today's architecture smaller and faster must stop, so computers will have to be reconceptualised: designs will use quantum effects deliberately (quantum bits and quantum computing), photonic interconnects, molecular or organic electronics, 3-D stacking instead of lateral scaling, and specialised architectures, rather than ever-smaller versions of the same transistor.

Limit 1, size and tunnelling. A transistor's gate is separated from its channel by a layer of insulator only a few atomic layers thick. As everything is scaled down the barrier the electrons must cross becomes comparable with the typical energy of an electron in the silicon, so tunnelling through the gate oxide becomes significant and the transistor leaks current even when it is nominally off.

There is also no room left for the metal connections: the interconnect has to shrink along with the devices, its resistance grows as its length grows and its cross-section falls, and the resulting resistance, together with the capacitance of the wire, sets an RC delay that stops the signals arriving quickly enough.

Limit 2, heat. Every time a node is charged or discharged, energy is dissipated in the resistance of the wires and the transistor itself, so the power drawn rises with both the number of switching events and the clock rate. On a small chip the power density becomes impossible to remove.

Limit 3, speed of the carriers. Electrons drift through the silicon at a speed limited by their mobility and the electric field, so there is a minimum time to charge and discharge each node and hence a shortest possible clock period. Making the wires longer, which more and more transistors per chip requires, makes this worse rather than better.

Limit 4, quantum. The uncertainty principle places a floor on how well the position and momentum of an electron can be known at the same time, and de Broglie's relationship ties its wavelength to its momentum, so a charge simply cannot be confined to a region much smaller than its own wavelength. At that point the idea of a well-defined on/off state inside a small box breaks down.

Why this forces a reconceptualisation. Every one of these limits is a consequence of the architecture itself, not of poor manufacturing, and they are reached at once: shrinking further makes the leakage, the wire delays and the quantum uncertainty worse while the heat to be removed goes up. Continuing to shrink and clock up the same silicon transistor is therefore not merely expensive, it is impossible, so the design has to change.

The directions the change actually takes are to use quantum effects deliberately, with qubits whose states are superpositions rather than definite 0s and 1s; to replace the wires with photonic interconnects carrying light; to build in three dimensions instead of scaling in two, stacking dies or active layers; to move to molecular or organic electronics with smaller switching units; and to abandon the general-purpose processor in favour of specialised architectures matched to each task.

items: 6-7 marks: provides a clear and concise explanation of the fundamental physics limitations that restrict the reduction in size and speed of digital integrated circuits, makes a clear connection between these size/speed limitations and the operation of computers, and makes a clear connection between the limitations and the need to fundamentally change the way computers are designed.
